abstract.para: &kdump; is not installed or enabled by default. Install and enable it so a crash produces a dump you can analyze afterward.

step.para: Install the &kdump; package. This pulls in kexec-tools and makedumpfile as dependencies:
Determine and, if needed, set the crash kernel memory reservation. See . The default KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL="auto" works for most systems.
Reboot so the crash kernel memory reservation takes effect:

section.title: Installing &kdump; on the immutable variant
section.para: On the immutable variant of &productnameshort;, install and enable &kdump; through transactional-update rather than plain zypper. Note that a plain zypper install does not fail on the read-only root file system either. &zypper; transparently wraps the operation through tukit, creating a new snapshot that only takes effect after a reboot. transactional-update setup-kdump is still the recommended way to install &kdump;, since it installs, enables and calibrates the crash kernel memory reservation in a single step:
To provide a custom crash kernel memory size instead of the automatically calculated one, append --crashkernel:
Reboot to activate the new snapshot and start using the updated &kdump; configuration:

note.title: /etc/sysconfig/kdump is directly editable on the immutable variant
note.para: Unlike most of the file system, /etc is its own writable subvolume on the immutable variant. Editing /etc/sysconfig/kdump directly with a text editor takes effect immediately, without needing transactional-update or a reboot, for options that do not require a new crash kernel memory reservation.

important.title: Changing the crash kernel memory reservation needs an explicit bootloader update
important.para: transactional-update setup-kdump sets KDUMP_UPDATE_BOOTLOADER="false". Unlike on a non-immutable system, kdump-commandline.service does not automatically update the boot loader on this variant even after a reboot: if the running kernel command line does not match what KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL expects, the service only logs a warning and exits with an error, leaving the old reservation in place. After editing KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL directly, push the change into the boot loader configuration explicitly:
Then reboot to activate the new snapshot. Only after this does the new crashkernel= value appear on the kernel command line.

section.title: What happens when &kdump; starts
section.para: When kdump.service starts, it loads the capture kernel and its initramfs into the reserved memory area. Afterward, kdump-commandline.service runs and checks whether the running kernel's command line (/proc/cmdline) already contains the crashkernel= options that kdumptool calibrate/KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL expect. If they are missing or different, and KDUMP_UPDATE_BOOTLOADER is set to its default of true, kdump-commandline.service updates the boot loader configuration through pbl(8) so the expected options are applied on the next boot.
To check whether the service found and applied any change:
Sample output, from a system that had no crash kernel memory reserved yet:
section.screen: Kdump expects these crashkernel= values on the kernel command line: crashkernel=72M,low crashkernel=394M,high (based on the output of 'kdumptool calibrate') No crashkernel= found in /proc/cmdline. Kdump can't be started. Updated the command line options in the bootloader. Changes will take effect on next boot.
section.para: If kdump-commandline.service updated the boot loader configuration, a reboot is required before the new crashkernel= values take effect and &kdump; can start capturing dumps.
